title: Exact leader election in anonymous networks

problem.name: Exact leader election in anonymous networks
problem.name_latex: Exact leader election in anonymous networks
problem.statement_latex: In a connected synchronous network of $n$ identical processors without unique identifiers, each knows $n$. Output bits summing to exactly one, in bounded time with zero error, on every topology. Complexity counts rounds and transmitted bits or qubits.
problem.statement_text: In a connected synchronous network of $n$ identical processors without unique identifiers, each knows $n$. Output bits summing to exactly one, in bounded time with zero error, on every topology. Complexity counts rounds and transmitted bits or qubits.

strength.description_latex: An exact-solvability separation in the anonymous-network model.
strength.description_text: An exact-solvability separation in the anonymous-network model.

evidence.description_latex: Quantum solvability and classical impossibility are unconditional.
evidence.description_text: Quantum solvability and classical impossibility are unconditional.

hardware.description_latex: Quantum links and polynomial coherent local resources are required.
hardware.description_text: Quantum links and polynomial coherent local resources are required.

quantum.headline_latex: $O(n)$ rounds and $O(mn^2)$ communication for $m$ links by Kobayashi--Matsumoto--Tani. Coherent symmetric-function computation enables exact symmetry breaking.
quantum.headline_text: $O(n)$ rounds and $O(mn^2)$ communication for $m$ links by Kobayashi–Matsumoto–Tani. Coherent symmetric-function computation enables exact symmetry breaking.

classical.headline_latex: Exact bounded-time leader election is impossible on general anonymous classical networks even with known n. Symmetric executions on symmetric topologies keep processors indistinguishable.
classical.headline_text: Exact bounded-time leader election is impossible on general anonymous classical networks even with known n. Symmetric executions on symmetric topologies keep processors indistinguishable.
